title: ability to swap meta learning algorithm with `caruana`
description:
would it be possible to add an option to blend candidates with glmnet or caruana? 

The caruana ensemble selection algorithm is a greedy iterative procedure that builds an ensemble by sequentially adding models from a pool with replacement to maximize a specific evaluation metric. This would provide an alternative to glmnet for tidymodels users. 

sidenote: this is to mimic the `TabArena` & `BeyondArea` ensemble method, which I am interested in replicating within tidymodels framework.

title: Error stacking classification models with `pr_auc`
description:
Hi - Stacks is proving very effective at improving model performance for me (using the output from `finetune::tune_sim_anneal()`). Thank you!

I am occasionally running into this problem though stacking classification models with metric `pr_auc`.

It's a bit of a contrived example to attempt to recreate the error:

(I also seem to get it when `num_members > 0`.)

``` r
library(tidymodels)
library(stacks)

data("tree_frogs")

tree_frogs <- tree_frogs |> 
  select(-c(clutch, latency)) |> 
  mutate(reflex = if_else(row_number() < 20, "low", "other"))

set.seed(1)

tree_frogs_split <- initial_split(tree_frogs)
tree_frogs_train <- training(tree_frogs_split)
tree_frogs_test  <- testing(tree_frogs_split)

folds <- vfold_cv(tree_frogs_train, v = 5)

tree_frogs_rec <- 
  recipe(reflex ~ ., data = tree_frogs_train) |> 
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), -reflex) |> 
  step_zv(all_predictors())

tree_frogs_wflow <- 
  workflow() |> 
  add_recipe(tree_frogs_rec)

ctrl_grid <- control_stack_grid()

rand_forest_spec <- 
  rand_forest(
    mtry = tune(),
    min_n = tune(),
    trees = 500
  ) %>%
  set_mode("classification") |> 
  set_engine("ranger")

rand_forest_wflow <-
  tree_frogs_wflow |> 
  add_model(rand_forest_spec)

rand_forest_res <- 
  tune_grid(
    object = rand_forest_wflow, 
    resamples = folds, 
    grid = 10,
    control = ctrl_grid
  )
#> i Creating pre-processing data to finalize unknown parameter: mtry

nnet_spec <-
  mlp(hidden_units = tune(), penalty = tune(), epochs = tune()) |> 
  set_mode("classification") |> 
  set_engine("nnet")

nnet_rec <- 
  tree_frogs_rec |> 
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

nnet_wflow <- 
  tree_frogs_wflow |> 
  add_model(nnet_spec) |> 
  update_recipe(nnet_rec)

nnet_res <-
  tune_grid(
    object = nnet_wflow, 
    resamples = folds, 
    grid = 10,
    control = ctrl_grid
  )

tree_frogs_model_st <- 
  stacks() |> 
  add_candidates(rand_forest_res) |> 
  add_candidates(nnet_res) |> 
  blend_predictions(
    metric = metric_set(pr_auc),
    mixture = 1,
    penalty = seq(0, 1, 0.1),
    ) |> 
  fit_members()
#> → A | warning: one multinomial or binomial class has fewer than 8  observations; dangerous ground
#> There were issues with some computations   A: x1
#> There were issues with some computations   A: x3
#> 

autoplot(tree_frogs_model_st)
#> Warning in ggplot2::scale_x_log10(): log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.
#> log-10 transformation introduced infinite values.
```

![](https://i.imgur.com/nycH9Nm.png)<!-- -->

``` r

length(tree_frogs_model_st$member_fits)
#> [1] 0

tree_frogs_model_st |> 
  augment(tree_frogs_test, type = "prob")
#> Error in `tidyr::pivot_wider()`:
#> ! Can't select columns past the end.
#> ℹ Location 3 doesn't exist.
#> ℹ There are only 2 columns.
```

title: Second event level in weights autoplot
description:
Simon hi - I wanted to label `autoplot("weights")` with the names of the engines. Use of `stacks:::top_coefs()` was very handy for getting the names! 

I was curious though why the weights plot then shows the coefficients for the second factor level rather than the first?

(Reprex based on the vignette example.)

``` r
library(tidymodels)
library(stacks)
library(bonsai)

data("tree_frogs")

tree_frogs <- tree_frogs |> 
  select(-c(clutch, latency)) |> 
  mutate(reflex = forcats::fct_other(reflex, keep = "low"))

# First event level = "low"
levels(tree_frogs$reflex)
#> [1] "low"   "Other"

set.seed(1)

tree_frogs_split <- initial_split(tree_frogs)
tree_frogs_train <- training(tree_frogs_split)
tree_frogs_test  <- testing(tree_frogs_split)

folds <- vfold_cv(tree_frogs_train, v = 5)

tree_frogs_rec <- 
  recipe(reflex ~ ., data = tree_frogs_train) |> 
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors(), -reflex) |> 
  step_zv(all_predictors())

tree_frogs_wflow <- 
  workflow() |> 
  add_recipe(tree_frogs_rec)

ctrl_grid <- control_stack_grid()

rand_forest_spec <- 
  rand_forest(
    mtry = tune(),
    min_n = tune(),
    trees = 5
  ) |> 
  set_mode("classification") |> 
  set_engine("ranger")

rand_forest_wflow <-
  tree_frogs_wflow |> 
  add_model(rand_forest_spec)

rand_forest_res <- 
  tune_grid(
    object = rand_forest_wflow, 
    resamples = folds, 
    grid = 10,
    control = ctrl_grid
  )
#> i Creating pre-processing data to finalize unknown parameter: mtry

aorsf_spec <- 
  rand_forest(
    mtry = tune(),
    min_n = tune(),
    trees = 500
  ) |> 
  set_mode("classification") |> 
  set_engine("aorsf")

aorsf_wflow <- 
  tree_frogs_wflow |> 
  add_model(aorsf_spec)

aorsf_res <-
  tune_grid(
    object = aorsf_wflow, 
    resamples = folds, 
    grid = 10,
    control = ctrl_grid
  )
#> i Creating pre-processing data to finalize unknown parameter: mtry

tree_frogs_model_st <- 
  stacks() |> 
  add_candidates(rand_forest_res, "ranger") |> 
  add_candidates(aorsf_res, "aorsf") |> 
  blend_predictions() |> 
  fit_members()

# To label the engines
members <- 
  stacks:::top_coefs(
    tree_frogs_model_st, 
    penalty = tree_frogs_model_st$penalty$penalty, 
    n = Inf
    ) |> 
  mutate(member = stringr::str_extract(member, "(?<=_).*(?=_1)"))

# Doesn't show the first event level "low"?
autoplot(tree_frogs_model_st, "weights") + 
  geom_label(
    aes(weight, nrow(members):1, label = member, fill = NULL),
    show.legend = FALSE, hjust = "inward",
    data = members
  )
```

title: Implement importance weighting in stacked ensembles
description:
## Feature

Similar to https://github.com/tidymodels/probably/issues/159.

When producing a stacked ensemble of predictions, although the base models may have been trained using importance weights, these weights don't seem to be passed on to the stacking procedure. In my use case I use importance weights to give additional weight to the minority class in a highly imbalanced dataset.

Here's a reprex - not a perfect test (comparing two "best" base learners with a stacked ensemble of several candidates) but demonstrates that the weights aren't being passed on and therefore the stacked ensemble is much less likely to predict the (highly weighted) minority class, compared to the base learners:

```
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
set.seed(100)

# Create noisy, imbalanced data, add weight column giving roughly equal overall weight
df <- caret::twoClassSim(n=1000, intercept = -12, linearVars = 2, noiseVars = 5,corrVars = 3, corrType = "AR1") |>
  dplyr::mutate(weights = dplyr::if_else(Class == "Class1",
                                         true =  0.15,
                                         false = 0.85)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(weights = hardhat::importance_weights(weights),
                Class = case_match(Class, "Class1" ~ "Majority",
                                   "Class2" ~ "Minority"))

# Create recipe and logistic regression specification
glm_recipe <- recipes::recipe(x = df, formula = Class ~ .)

glm_spec <- parsnip::logistic_reg(mode = "classification",
                                  engine = "glm")

# Combine into workflow
glm_wf <- workflows::workflow(preprocessor = glm_recipe,
                              spec = glm_spec) |>
  workflows::add_case_weights(col = weights)

# Now let's do an xgBoost one
# Don't include all variables so it's not amazingly accurate
xgb_recipe <-  recipes::recipe(x = df,
                               formula = Class ~ Linear1 + Linear2 + Nonlinear1 + Noise1 + Noise2 + weights)

xgb_spec <- parsnip::boost_tree(mode = "classification",
                                engine = "xgboost",
                                trees = 100,
                                tree_depth = tune(),
                                learn_rate = 0.1)

xgb_wf <- workflows::workflow(preprocessor = xgb_recipe,
                              spec = xgb_spec) |>
  workflows::add_case_weights(col = weights)

# Create resamples for model fitting
resamples <- rsample::vfold_cv(data = df,
                               v = 5,
                               strata = Class)

# Cross-validate the models
glm_cv <- fit_resamples(glm_wf, resamples = resamples, control = control_stack_resamples())
xgb_cv <- tune_grid(xgb_wf, resamples = resamples, control = control_stack_resamples())

# Stack the ensemble
model_stack <- stacks() |>
  add_candidates(candidates = glm_cv) |>
  add_candidates(candidates = xgb_cv) |>
  blend_predictions() |>
  fit_members()

# Add stacked predictions to dataframe
df <- df |>
  bind_cols(predict(model_stack, df, type = "prob")|>
              rename(.pred_Majority_stack =.pred_Majority,
                     .pred_Minority_stack =.pred_Minority))

# Fit best individual models
best_glm <- fit_best(glm_cv)
best_xgb <- fit_best(xgb_cv)

# Append individual model predictions to the data
df <- df |>
  bind_cols(predict(best_glm, df, type = "prob") |>
                    rename(.pred_Majority_glm =.pred_Majority,
                           .pred_Minority_glm =.pred_Minority)) |>
  bind_cols(predict(best_xgb, df, type = "prob") |>
              rename(.pred_Majority_xgb =.pred_Majority,
                     .pred_Minority_xgb =.pred_Minority))

# Bring together and visualise the predictions
 df |>
  select(Class, starts_with(".pred_Min")) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with(".pred_Min"),
               names_to = "model",
               values_to = ".pred_min",
               names_prefix = ".pred_Minority_") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = .pred_min,colour= model,  fill = model)) + 
  geom_density(alpha = 0.2) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(x = "Predicted probability of being in the minority class") +
   facet_wrap(~Class, nrow = 2)

```

title: Model performance metrics: ROC, Conf Matrix, compare to single models
description:
Hi tidymodels/stacks team, 

I **love** the `stacks` package but cannot find any documentation to obtain model performance metrics, akin to the tidymodels workflow pipeline. 

I am interested in comparing the model performance of the stacks model to my **single** model workflows generated using `workflowsets`. 

For this, I would like to plot ROC and obtain sensitivity/specificity and confusion matrix values, not just obtain a single AUC at the end. 

This is my current code in {stacks}. Any help would be greatly appreciated. Thanks! 

```{r}
########################################################################
# Define resampling and basic recipe 
########################################################################
set.seed(1234)
cores         <- parallel::detectCores() - 1 # determine number of cores
d_folds       <- vfold_cv(d, v = 10, repeats = 5, strata = status) # creates cross validation
keep_pred     <- control_resamples(save_pred = TRUE, save_workflow = TRUE)
ctrl_grid     <- control_stack_grid() # use same control settings as in numeric response setting 
log_recipe    <- recipe(status ~., data = d) %>% step_log(all_predictors()) 
status_wkfl   <- workflow() %>% add_recipe(log_recipe)

########################################################################
# Define models to predict status
########################################################################
logistic_reg_spec_tuned <- logistic_reg() %>% # no tuning parameters
	set_engine("glm") %>%
	set_mode("classification") 

boost_tree_spec_tuned <- boost_tree() %>%
  set_args(tree_depth = 4, learn_rate = 0.001, loss_reduction = 0.005, mtry = 2, # stop iter
           min_n = 27, sample_size = 0.8125, trees = 10000) %>% 
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("xgboost")

nearest_neighbor_spec_tuned <- nearest_neighbor() %>% 
  set_args(neighbors = 14, dist_power = 1.525, weight_func = "gaussian") %>% 
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("kknn")

discrim_linear_spec_tuned <- discrim_linear() %>% # no tuning parameters
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("MASS")

naive_bayes_spec_tuned <- naive_Bayes(smoothness = 0.5, Laplace = 1.75) %>%
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("naivebayes")

discrim_quad_spec_tuned <- discrim_quad() %>% # no tuning parameters
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("MASS")

rand_forest_spec_tuned <- rand_forest() %>%
  set_args(trees = 10000, mtry = 2, min_n = 7) %>%
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("ranger",
             importance = "permutation",
             num.threads = cores,
             probability = TRUE,
             seed = 1234) 

svm_linear_spec_tuned <- svm_linear() %>%
  set_args(cost = 0.002, margin = 0.167) %>% 
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("kernlab")

########################################################################
# Create {workflowsets} object
########################################################################
antibody_wkfl_tuned <- workflow_set(
  preproc = list(log = log_recipe),
  models = list(
    rand_forest = rand_forest_spec_tuned, 
    logistic_reg = logistic_reg_spec_tuned, 
    discrim_linear = discrim_linear_spec_tuned, 
    discrim_quad = discrim_quad_spec_tuned, 
    nearest_neighbor = nearest_neighbor_spec_tuned, 
    boost_tree = boost_tree_spec_tuned, 
    svm_linear = svm_linear_spec_tuned,
    naive_bayes = naive_bayes_spec_tuned
  )
)

########################################################################
# Run resampling
########################################################################
grid_ctrl <- control_grid(
      save_pred = TRUE,
      parallel_over = "everything",
      save_workflow = TRUE
   )

final_models <-
   antibody_wkfl_tuned %>%
   workflow_map(
      seed = 1234,
      resamples = d_folds,
      grid = 25,
      control = grid_ctrl
   )

########################################################################
# Putting my stack together 
########################################################################
antibody_wkfl_stack <- 
  # initialise the stack 
  stacks() %>% 
  # add candidate members i.e., {workflowsets} object
  add_candidates(final_models)

as_tibble(antibody_wkfl_stack)

########################################################################
# Blend the stack 
########################################################################
antibody_wkfl_blend <- 
  antibody_wkfl_stack_nofit %>% 
  blend_predictions()

antibody_wkfl_blend

# view roc_auc for various penalty parameters:
antibody_wkfl_blend$metrics %>% filter(.metric == "roc_auc")

########################################################################
# Fit the stack 
########################################################################
antibody_wkfl_fit_stack <- 
  # initialise the stack 
  stacks() %>% 
  # add candidate members i.e., {workflowsets} object
  add_candidates(final_models) %>% 
  # determine how to combine predictions
  blend_predictions() %>% 
  # fit the candidates with non-zero stacking coefficients
  fit_members() 

antibody_wkfl_fit_stack

########################################################################
# Evaluate stack performance 
########################################################################
# Plot: Trade-off between minimising number of members and optimising performance 
autoplot(antibody_wkfl_stack)

# Plot: Weights
autoplot(antibody_wkfl_stack, type = "weights")

# Collect parameters e.g., for random forest model 
collect_parameters(antibody_wkfl_stack, "log_rand_forest")

```

title: Unclear error message of add_candidates(): The inputted `candidates` argument was not generated
description:
Using `add_candidates()`, I obtained the following error message: 

> Error in `add_candidates()`:
! The inputted `candidates` argument was not generated with the appropriate control settings. Please see
  `control_stack()`.

After a lot of guessing, I understood that the problem was that I had generated `control_grid(save_pred = FALSE)` but I don't think the error message will lead a user to that conclusion?

1. The error message leads to   `control_stack()`, which doesn't seem to exist?
2. If the user goes to `control_stack_grid()` instead, the help file has no example, nor description of inputs of the function, making it very hard to diagnostic the problem

So based on this, it does not seem to me that the actual error message will lead the user to understand that the problem was using `control_grid(save_pred = FALSE)`?

Thanks!

title: audit for backticked package names
description:
In many places in stacks, the package name is written "`stacks`" rather than "stacks" (i.e. there are backticks before and after). Per [tidy style](https://style.tidyverse.org/index.html), package names don't need backticks.

Here's an example GitHub search:

https://github.com/search?q=repo%3Atidymodels%2Fstacks%20%22%60stacks%60%22&type=code

Let's search for tidymodels and tidyverse package names and make sure they're not backticked.

The part that makes this a little more tricky than a Find and Replace is knowing when the thing should actually be backticked vs. not. If the text is definitely referencing stacks _as a package_, take the backticks away. If there's e.g. a reference to the `stacks()` function rather than the package stacks, leave it as is (making sure to include parentheses following function names if needed). Be sure to `devtools::document()` and/or `devtools::build_readme()` before putting in the PR!

title: reduce size of final model_stack for making predictions
description:
After finalizing a model_stack with fit_members(), I get a large object (~13.5 GB) that is inconvenient to use in my specific research production setting. Is there a way to trim the final stack object while still maintaining it's wonderfully simple predict() implementation?

My initial thought was to simply remove the "data_stack" and "splits" (~6.5 GB and ~5.2 GB, respectively, out of the 13.5 GB total). As far as I can tell the splits aren't require in predict.model_stack(), but I see that the data_stack is being called to retrieve the outcome when type = "class". 

If I'm only interesting in type = "prob", I can remove the data_stack and splits elements using the proper indexing, and still pass this trimmed object to predict.model_stack() without consequence (I think). 

But maybe there is a more elegant solution to this. 

I've attached a reprex example below. 

``` r
# HOUSEKEEPING ####
rm(list = ls(all = TRUE)) # clean house
# CRAN libraries
library(tidyverse) # install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidymodels) # install.packages("tidymodels")
library(stacks) # install.packages("stacks")


# DEFINE SEED ####
seed <- 42


# DEFINE SET ####
tree_frogs_class_train <- tree_frogs %>%
    dplyr::select(-c(clutch, latency))


# SET UP RESAMPLING ####
set.seed(seed)
cv_folds <- tree_frogs_class_train %>% rsample::vfold_cv(v = 5)


# BUILD MODELS ####
mod_svmlinear <- parsnip::svm_linear(cost = tune(), margin = tune()) %>%
    parsnip::set_engine("kernlab") %>%
    parsnip::set_mode("classification")

mod_elasticnet <- parsnip::logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) %>%
    parsnip::set_engine("glmnet") %>%
    parsnip::set_mode("classification")


# BUILD RECIPE ####
recipe_set <- recipes::recipe(hatched ~ ., data = tree_frogs_class_train) %>%
    recipes::step_dummy(recipes::all_nominal(), -hatched) %>%
    recipes::step_zv(recipes::all_predictors()) %>%
    recipes::step_normalize(recipes::all_numeric())


# CREATE WORKFLOW ####
workflow_set <- workflowsets::workflow_set(
    preproc = list(recipe_set),
    models = list(
        svm_linear = mod_svmlinear,
        elasticnet = mod_elasticnet
    )
) 


# TUNING ####
res_tune <- workflow_set %>%
    workflowsets::workflow_map(
        seed = seed,
        resamples = cv_folds,
        fn = "tune_grid",
        grid = 25,
        metrics = yardstick::metric_set(roc_auc),
        control = tune::control_grid(
            save_pred = TRUE,
            save_workflow = TRUE,
            verbose = FALSE,
            allow_par = FALSE,
        )
    )


# DEFINE ENSEMBLE STACK ####
stack_finalized <- stacks::stacks() %>%
    stacks::add_candidates(res_tune) %>%
    stacks::blend_predictions() %>%
    stacks::fit_members()


# CHECK THE ELEMENTS OF THE MODEL_STACK ####
stack_finalized %>% names()
#>  [1] "model_defs"    "coefs"         "penalty"       "metrics"      
#>  [5] "equations"     "cols_map"      "model_metrics" "train"        
#>  [9] "mode"          "outcome"       "data_stack"    "splits"       
#> [13] "member_fits"


# CHECK THE SIZE OF THE WHOLE MODEL_STACK ####
stack_finalized %>%
    object.size() %>%
    format("MB")
#> [1] "2 Mb"


# CHECK THE SIZE OF THE MODEL_STACK WITHOUT data_stack AND splits ####
stack_finalized[-c(11, 12)] %>%
    object.size() %>%
    format("MB")
#> [1] "0.9 Mb"


# TRIM THE MODEL_STACK
stack_finalized_trimmed <- stack_finalized[-c(11, 12)]


# COMPARE THE CLASSES ####
stack_finalized  %>% class()
#> [1] "linear_stack" "model_stack"  "list"
stack_finalized_trimmed %>% class() # just a list
#> [1] "list"


# MAKE PREDICTIONS WITH WHOLE MODEL_STACK ####
stack_finalized %>%
    stacks::predict.model_stack(new_data = tree_frogs_class_train, type = "prob") %>%
```

title: Generalizing the stacks API to enable more customization
description:
Hi @simonpcouch,

I love the `{stacks}` package and over the last several months have thought about it quite a bit and whether there is room to broaden the API to be more flexible. It seems to me that the current API is _opinionated_ on a few things:

1. The stacking model must be Ridge/LASSO/ElasticNet
2. The resampling is done via bootstrapping
3. The training routine is `tune::tune_grid()`

I am wondering if there is interest in a function one level _lower_ than `blend_predictions()` that is more flexible on the three design considerations described above. Most importantly, a more general API for stacking would allow users to take advantage of the __huge__ breadth of models available through `parsnip` et al. for stacking predictions (e.g., random forest, XGBoost, etc.). In theory, any model that supports the `mode` would be a candidate for the stacking model.

Without actually considering the implementation too much, I image some function, let's call it `stack_predictions()`, because I don't have a better name off the top of my head, that looks something like:

```r
stack_predictions(
  data_stack,
  model = parsnip::linear_reg(engine = "glmnet", penalty = tune(), mixture = tune())
  fn = tune::tune_grid,
  resamples = rsample::bootstrap(times = 25),
  control = tune::control_grid(),
  ... # passed on to `fn` (metric, grid, param_info)
)
```

What do you think? This way the user can control the stacking more finely and `blend_predictions()` would be a special case of `stack_predictions()` and could potentially call this function internally. That way if you wanted to stack with a random forest, tune with `{finetune}`, and use 100 Monte Carlo resamples, you could do something like:

```r
stacks() |>
  add_candidates(wflow_set_results) |>
  stack_predictions(
    model = parsnip::rand_forest(...),
    fn = finetune::tune_race_anova,
    resamples = rsample::mc_cv(times = 100)
  )
```

I have thought about this a few times and figured it was worth going full stream of consciousness and laying it all out for you to think about. Happy to chat more and think about this more thoroughly. As always, happy to contribute and not just request features.

While I'm thinking about it, in order to support more stacking models, there needs to be a way to define what it means to be a "non-zero stacking coefficient" for models for which coefficients don't really exist (e.g., Random Forest). Perhaps for tree-based models, if a model's prediction are used for a split in any tree, it is "non-zero" - this requires some more thinking.

title: blend_predictions does not support gam models with a custom formula
description:
It does not seem to be possible to use a gam model with workflowset.

When using a gam model in a workflowset, the custom formula is specified using the formula argument of
workflowsets::update_workflow_model()

However stack_workflow() only uses extract_spec_parsnip() and extract_preprocessor() so it never saves the custom formula into the candidate.  

```r
library(magrittr)
# generate data
x <- data.frame(date = seq(from = as.POSIXct("2000-01-01"), to = as.POSIXct("2020-01-01"), by = "DSTday"))
x <- cbind(x, x = runif(n = NROW(x)), weekday = lubridate::wday(x$date))
x$y <- dplyr::lead(x$x, n = 1) + sin(as.numeric(x$weekday)) / 10
#
# recipe
p <- recipes::recipe(x, formula = y ~ date + x + weekday) %>%
  recipes::update_role(date, new_role = "date")
#
# sliding resampling
r <- rsample::sliding_period(data = x, index = date, period = "month", lookback = 120, assess_stop = 12, step = 12)
# workflow sets for lm and gam formula
m.lm <- parsnip::linear_reg()
m.gam <- parsnip::gen_additive_mod(mode = "regression")
ws <- workflowsets::workflow_set(preproc = list(p = p), models = list(lm = m.lm, gam = m.gam), cross = T) %>%
  workflowsets::update_workflow_model(id = "p_gam", spec = m.gam, formula = y ~ s(x) + s(weekday, bs = "cc", k = 7))
wfs <- workflowsets::workflow_map(
  object = ws,
  fn = "fit_resamples",
  resamples = r,
  control = tune::control_resamples(save_pred = T, save_workflow = T)
)

# stacking
s <- stacks::stacks() %>%
  stacks::add_candidates(wfs) %>%
  stacks::blend_predictions(penalty = 1e-8, mixture = 0, times = 2)

stacks::fit_members(s)
# Error in { :
#     task 2 failed - "`fit()` must be used with GAM models (due to its use of formulas)."
```

title: Cross-validation score
description:
Related to #130.

When analysing the stacks I build, I want to easily obtain the CV score and not the score for the test dataset.

Instead of collect_metrics() I need to do something like this:

```
ensemble_cv <- 
    stacks() %>%
    add_candidates(glmnet_tune %>% filter_parameters(parameters = select_best(glmnet_tune))) %>%
    add_candidates(xgboost_tune %>% filter_parameters(parameters = select_best(xgboost_tune))) %>%
    blend_predictions() 

result <- folds$splits %>% map_df(function(x) {
  ensemble_cv$train <- analysis(x)
  ensemble_cv %>%
    fit_members() %>%
    predict(assessment(x)) %>%
    bind_cols(assessment(x), .) %>%
    rmse(.pred, med_house_val)
})

result %>% 
  summarize(
    mean = mean(.estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    n = sum(!is.na(.estimator)),
    std_err = sd(.estimate, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(n)
  )
```

I already have CV scores for glmnet and xgboost and I see that I can trust them more than a single score on the test dataset.

What do you think?

```
    grid = 4,

stopCluster(cls)
```

title: No `augment` method for stacks
description:
As pointed out in rstudio/vetiver-r#170, we don't yet have `augment` methods for stacks objects:

``` r
library(tidymodels)
library(stacks)

tree_frogs_class <- 
    tree_frogs %>%
    dplyr::select(-c(clutch, latency))

tree_frogs_class_split <- initial_split(tree_frogs_class)
tree_frogs_class_train <- training(tree_frogs_class_split)
tree_frogs_class_test  <- testing(tree_frogs_class_split)

log_st <-
    stacks() %>%
    add_candidates(log_res_nn) %>%
    add_candidates(log_res_rf) %>%
    blend_predictions() %>%
    fit_members()

## OK:
predict(log_st, tree_frogs_class_test)
#> # A tibble: 303 × 1
#>    .pred_class
#>    <fct>      
#>  1 yes        
#>  2 yes        
#>  3 yes        
#>  4 no         
#>  5 no         
#>  6 no         
#>  7 no         
#>  8 yes        
#>  9 no         
#> 10 no         
#> # … with 293 more rows

## not OK:
augment(log_st, tree_frogs_class_test)
#> Error: No augment method for objects of class linear_stack
```

<sup>Created on 2023-01-11 with [reprex v2.0.2](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

We show folks how to set up vetiver model monitoring using `augment()`, so this would be nice to have.

title: saveRDS / readRDS issue with 'lightgbm' engine
description:
### The Problem: saveRDS / readRDS for lightgbm engine

 * I'm having trouble when stacking an ensemble model with "set_engine = 'lightgbm'", if we want to save the model as an RDS and read in later, the model will not predict. 
 
 * Error message: "Error in predictor$predict(data = data, start_iteration = start_iteration,  : 
  Attempting to use a Booster which no longer exists. This can happen if you have called Booster$finalize() or if this Booster was saved with saveRDS(). To avoid this error in the future, use saveRDS.lgb.Booster() or Booster$save_model() to save lightgbm Boosters."
  
* Seems to be an underlying issue with lightgbm but hoping this could be handled in stacks, maybe this bug should be posted on bonsai. Would like to easily stack cubist + lightgbm without doing a workaround.


## Reproducible example
``` r
library(stacks)
library(tidymodels)
library(workflows)
library(recipes)
library(bonsai)

library(dplyr)

in_garden <- 315159
set.seed(in_garden)
r <- rnorm(n = 999)

some_data <- data.frame(
  A = r,
  B = r + 1.3,
  C = r ^ 2
)

# introduce cv folds, recipes, param tune, and stacks --

data_split <- initial_split(some_data, 
                            prop = .75, 
                            strata = A) 

training <- training(data_split) 
testing <- testing(data_split)

# cross-validations ---
folds <- vfold_cv(training, strata = A, v = 5)


model_recipe <-
  recipe(A ~ ., training) %>%
  step_nzv(all_nominal()) %>% 
  step_dummy(all_nominal()) %>%
  step_zv(all_predictors())

# gbm - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - 
gbm_results <-
    tune_grid(
    workflow() %>%
      add_recipe(model_recipe) %>%
      add_model(
        boost_tree(
             trees = tune(),
             mtry = tune()) %>% 
          set_engine("lightgbm", nthread = 8) %>% 
          set_mode("regression")
      ),
    resamples = folds,
    grid = expand.grid(
      trees = c(5, 50),
      mtry = c(1, 2)
    ),
    control = control_stack_grid(),
    metrics = metric_set(rmse)
  )

# ensembling - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - 

candidate_stack <- 
  stacks() %>%
 # add_candidates(cube_results) %>%
  add_candidates(gbm_results)

ensemble_mixed_model <- candidate_stack %>% 
                          blend_predictions()

ensemble_mixed_model_fitted <- ensemble_mixed_model %>% 
                                fit_members()
#> [LightGBM] [Warning] num_threads is set=0, nthread=8 will be ignored. Current value: num_threads=0



# save/read RDS & predict issue - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - 
my_temp <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")

saveRDS(ensemble_mixed_model_fitted, file = my_temp)
remove(ensemble_mixed_model_fitted)

ensemble_mixed_model_fitted <- readRDS(my_temp)


testing %>% 
  bind_cols(predict(ensemble_mixed_model_fitted, .))
#> Error in predictor$predict(data = data, start_iteration = start_iteration, : Attempting to use a Booster which no longer exists. This can happen if you have called Booster$finalize() or if this Booster was saved with saveRDS(). To avoid this error in the future, use saveRDS.lgb.Booster() or Booster$save_model() to save lightgbm Boosters.
```

title: JOSS Review for stacks: Stacked Ensemble Modeling with Tidy Data Principles #4471
description:
Dear @simonpcouch,

Your paper is submitted to JOSS ([https://github.com/openjournals/joss-reviews/issues/4471](https://github.com/openjournals/joss-reviews/issues/4471)), is well-written and pretty understandable. But I think it needs some minor additions:

* The statement of need and the mechanism of the package look enough convincing, but there is no link or example of how it can be used. To link or cite [the vignettes](https://stacks.tidymodels.org/articles/basics.html) of the {stacks} may be useful for the readers.

* It is indicated the main superiority of the {stacks} is its tidy mechanism that utilizes the consistent and unified interface of the {tidymodels} packages to implement a generalized and concise grammar for model stacking. In the section "Comparison to Other Softwares", some specific comparisons between its alternatives may be given besides general comments.

Thanks,
Mustafa

title: [JOSS] Comments

Hi all!

I'm currently reviewing the JOSS submission for stacks (https://github.com/openjournals/joss-reviews/issues/4471). I think the paper is *very* well written and is worthy of publication at JOSS. 

Below is an overview of all my relatively minor comments. I'm happy to discuss them in this thread or in a separate issue, if need be.

Robrecht

---

- [x] State of the field: I think it would be worthwhile to include mlr3 in the comparison to other packages.
- [x] State of the field: The 'Statement of need' and 'Comparison to other packages' sections only discuss model stacking / ensemble modelling in the context of R. Please also discuss the state of the field outside the R ecosystem?
- [x] References: It probably makes sense to cite the academic paper for superlearner (https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.2202/1544-6115.1309/html?) and H2O (https://www.automl.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/AutoML_2020_paper_61.pdf?).

title: handling columns called `class`
description:
stacks currently fails when a `classification` outcome name is `class`. The issue arises here:

https://github.com/tidymodels/stacks/blob/4843385f031790cb16c6ab5713926551f9897cde/R/add_candidates.R#L282-L285

The logic here selects _class probability_ predictions and the true outcome and gets rid of columns with `.pred_class` (i.e. the columns with _hard class_ predictions), as the ensemble doesn't make use of hard class predictions in stacking models. {tune} (or some other dependency) labels hard class prediction columns as `.pred_colname`.

``` r
library(tidymodels)
library(workflowsets)
library(stacks)

# need devel modeldata for sim_classification
# devtools::install_github("tidymodels/modeldata")
library(modeldata)

x <- sim_classification(100)

spec_lasso <-
  logistic_reg(engine = 'glmnet', penalty = tune(), mixture = 1)

rec <- 
  recipe(class ~ ., x) %>% 
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

res <- tune_grid(
  spec_lasso,
  preprocessor = rec,
  resamples = vfold_cv(x, 2),
  grid = 2,
  control = control_stack_grid()
)

stacks() %>% 
  add_candidates(res) %>% 
  blend_predictions()
```

title: Saved model memory issue
description:
## The problem

I'm having trouble with saving a stacked xgb model object in local folder for later use. The issue is that the object somehow expands in size and does not fit into RAM when read back to new session. I have tried to butchering but it does not seem to help much.

Im not sure if this is due to stacks, butcher or simply my approach. Here is an example with a lot smaller dataset than the one I struggle with but the relative increase in size is of the same magnitude.

Thanks,

## Reproducible example

```r
library(tidymodels)
library(butcher)
library(stacks)
library(finetune)
library(readr)

set.seed(123)
cars <- mtcars[rep(1:32, each = 1000),] 
split <- initial_split(cars)
train <- training(split)
test <- testing(split)

valid_metric <- 'rmse' 
metrics <- metric_set(!!sym(valid_metric))

base_spec <- 
  boost_tree( trees = 500,
              min_n = tune(),
              mtry = tune(),
              sample_size = tune(),
              learn_rate = tune(),
              loss_reduction = tune()) %>% 
  set_mode("regression") %>% 
  set_engine("xgboost") 

base_recipe <- 
  recipe(vs ~ ., data = train %>% dplyr::slice(0))

wf <-
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(base_recipe) %>% 
  add_model(base_spec) 


tuned <- tune_race_anova(
  wf,
  resamples = vfold_cv(train, v = 5),
  grid = 15,
  metrics = metrics,
  control = control_race(verbose_elim = TRUE, save_pred = TRUE, save_workflow = TRUE)
)
#> i Creating pre-processing data to finalize unknown parameter: mtry
#> i Racing will minimize the rmse metric.
#> i Resamples are analyzed in a random order.
#> i Fold5:  9 eliminated;  6 candidates remain.
#> i Fold1:  4 eliminated;  2 candidates remain.

stacked <- 
  stacks() %>%
  add_candidates(tuned) %>%
  blend_predictions(metric  = metrics) %>%
  fit_members()


lobstr::obj_size(stacked)
#> 9,237,216 B
lobstr::obj_size(butcher(stacked))
#> 8,452,936 B

readr::write_rds(stacked, file = 'stack.rds')
readr::write_rds(butcher(stacked), file = 'stack_butch.rds')

back_in_r <- readr::read_rds('stack.rds')
back_in_r_butch <- readr::read_rds('stack_butch.rds')

lobstr::obj_size(back_in_r)
#> 462,770,208 B
lobstr::obj_size(back_in_r_butch)
#> 429,055,960 B

as.numeric(lobstr::obj_size(back_in_r_butch))/as.numeric(lobstr::obj_size(butcher(stacked))) #50x more in size
#> [1] 50.75822
```

title: stacks compatability with DALEXtra::explain_tidymodels
description:
## Feature

Would it be possible to add a feature to allow a stacks model to be used with the DALEXtra::explain_tidymodels function? The initial error below is because the DALEXtra::explain_tidymodels function looks for a "trained" flag in the stacks object, but I don't believe the predict calls are in the same spot for a stacks model as it would be for a regular tidymodel.

``` r
library(tidymodels)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip
#> Warning: package 'broom' was built under R version 4.0.4
#> Warning: package 'recipes' was built under R version 4.0.4
#> Warning: package 'workflowsets' was built under R version 4.0.4
#> Warning: package 'yardstick' was built under R version 4.0.4
library(stacks)
#> Warning: package 'stacks' was built under R version 4.0.4
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(DALEXtra)
#> Warning: package 'DALEXtra' was built under R version 4.0.4
#> Loading required package: DALEX
#> Warning: package 'DALEX' was built under R version 4.0.5
#> Welcome to DALEX (version: 2.2.1).
#> Find examples and detailed introduction at: http://ema.drwhy.ai/
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'DALEX'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:dplyr':
#> 
#>     explain
#> Anaconda not found on your computer. Conda related functionality such as create_env.R and condaenv and yml parameters from explain_scikitlearn will not be available

data("tree_frogs")

# subset the data
tree_frogs <- tree_frogs %>%
  filter(!is.na(latency)) %>%
  select(-c(clutch, hatched))

# some setup: resampling and a basic recipe
set.seed(1)
tree_frogs_split <- initial_split(tree_frogs)
tree_frogs_train <- training(tree_frogs_split)
tree_frogs_test  <- testing(tree_frogs_split)

set.seed(1)
folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(tree_frogs_train, v = 5)

tree_frogs_rec <- recipe(latency ~ ., data = tree_frogs_train)

ctrl_grid <- control_stack_grid()

#KNN
tree_frogs_knn <-
  nearest_neighbor(mode = "regression",
                   engine = "kknn",
                   neighbors = tune())

#Decision Tree
tree_frogs_cart <- 
  decision_tree(mode = "regression",
                engine = "rpart",
                cost_complexity = tune(),
                min_n = tune(),
                tree_depth = tune())

#Workflowset
tree_frogs_workflowsets <-
  workflow_set(
    preproc = list(rec = tree_frogs_rec),
    models = list(knn = tree_frogs_knn,
                  cart = tree_frogs_cart))

res_grid <-
  tree_frogs_workflowsets %>%
  workflow_map(
    'tune_grid',
    metrics = metric_set(rmse),
    resamples = folds,
    control = ctrl_grid,
    verbose = TRUE
  )
#> i 1 of 2 tuning:     rec_knn
#> Warning: package 'rlang' was built under R version 4.0.4
#> Warning: package 'vctrs' was built under R version 4.0.4
#> v 1 of 2 tuning:     rec_knn (5.1s)
#> i 2 of 2 tuning:     rec_cart
#> v 2 of 2 tuning:     rec_cart (18s)

tree_frogs_stack <-
  stacks() %>% 
  add_candidates(res_grid) %>%
  blend_predictions() %>% 
  fit_members()

tree_frogs_explainer <-
  explain_tidymodels(
    tree_frogs_stack,
    data = select(tree_frogs_train, -latency),
    y =  pull(tree_frogs_train, latency))
#> Error in !model$trained: invalid argument type
```

title: fit_members needs a new_data option
description:
## Feature

When building a stack it is natural that all the work is done on the training set, so that we can check accuracy on the test set. But after all that, we often want the very last step to train the model on the full data.

For example, if we were building a random forest, we might do something like:

``` r
# imagine we already have a workflow, data_split and tuning done, we'd want to check what our accuracy might be using this model

rf_wf |>
  finalize_workflow(whatever you choose) |>
  last_fit(data_split) |>
  pull(.metrics)

# now we might want to train the model on the full data, ready for entirely new data, rather than limit training to the training set

rf_model <- rf_wf |>
  finalize_workflow(whatever you choose) |>
  fit(full_data)
```
This is possible thanks to `fit` having a `new_data` argument. However, with `fit_members` there isn't this possibility so the final model has to remain trained only on the training set.

```r
control_stack_grid2 <- function(...) {
```

title: add_candidates() takes a long time to collect predictions
description:
I was recently trying to use `stacks` to create a stacked model for a multinomial regression problem with 20,000 observations, 20 classes for the outcome of interest, and four sets of tuned candidate models trained via 5-fold cross-validation. Overall there should have been about 90 candidate models available. However I could never get past the `add_candidates()` step. The computer was running for hours and hours and never even got to blending the predictions.

I believe the issue is caused by how `add_candidates()` relies on `tune::collect_predictions()` to extract the assessment set predictions for each candidate model.

https://github.com/tidymodels/stacks/blob/0985737a90c3f51d6a82a503ad1fe85c5a18884d/R/add_candidates.R#L477-L478

When `summarize = TRUE`, `collect_predictions()` uses the internal [`prob_summarize()`](https://github.com/tidymodels/tune/blob/2ce6a434ec0dc46f9ac373842503e6587cb16671/R/collect.R#L186-L253) function to generate average probabilities for each observation. Based on my understanding of `collect_predictions()`, this is necessary when there is more than one assessment set prediction for a single observation in a single candidate model. However in the case of standard cross-validation, will there be more than one assessment set prediction per observation per candidate model?

Consider the example below. The output of `collect_predictions()` is essentially the same whether or not one summarizes the predictions. The only significant difference I see is the `id` column indicating the fold is dropped, and the column order is adjusted. Otherwise they contain the same rows and same predicted probabilities, but collection with summarize is 18 times slower.

``` r
library(tidymodels)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':

#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip
library(stacks)
library(palmerpenguins)

set.seed(123)

# create folds
penguins_folds <- vfold_cv(data = penguins)

# create basic model and tune over penalty
tuned <- recipe(species ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm +
  flipper_length_mm, data = penguins) %>%
  step_impute_mean(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  workflow(multinom_reg(engine = "glmnet", penalty = tune(), mixture = 0)) %>%
  tune_grid(penguins_folds,
    grid = 10,
    control = control_stack_grid()
  )

# collect_predictions
tuned_bm <- microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  summarize_true = collect_predictions(tuned, summarize = TRUE),
  summarize_false = collect_predictions(tuned, summarize = FALSE)
)

# collection with summarize takes much longer
```

title: Enable add_candidate() to construct members from individual data columns
description:
## Feature

Currently, new candidates are added to a `stacks()` object using `add_candidates()` by providing a fitted `tune_results` or `resample_results` object.

Let's assume that aside form all the model predictions I also have an expert estimates in my data as a separate variable/column (similar to the prediction model, the human was also asked to give an educated guess for the response). Would it be possible to use `add_candidates()` in a way that also allows me to integrate expert estimates (depicted by single column in my underlying data) as an additional "base model" into my meta model, i.e. the stacked model? In particular, I am curious how much weight the expert estimate would be assigned to by the meta learner. I am not sure though, how this could look like programmatically...

title: fit_models() fails on multiclass predictions if the classes aren't valid R variable names
description:
## The problem

When predicting a multiclass factor, `fit_members()` fails if the outcome includes levels that aren't valid R variable names (e.g. they include spaces or punctuation). It fails with the message:

```
task 1 failed - "`parameters` objects cannot be created from this type of object."
``` 

A little experimentation indicates that this is because a full_join fails and leaves NAs in a "name" column whenever an outcome level is not a valid variable name (see below).

## Reproducible example

```r
library(tidymodels)
library(stacks)
library(palmerpenguins)

# change the species so that it has a - in it (any special character will do).
dat <- penguins %>%
  mutate(species = paste0(species, "-1"))

# Create three versions with different penalty parameters
tuned <- recipe(species ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm +
                  flipper_length_mm, data = dat) %>%
  step_impute_mean(all_numeric_predictors()) %>%
  workflow(multinom_reg(engine = "glmnet", penalty = tune())) %>%
  tune_grid(dat %>% vfold_cv(3),
            metrics = metric_set(mn_log_loss),
            grid = crossing(penalty = c(.0001, .001, .01)),
            control = control_stack_grid())

# Blending the predictions works
blended <- stacks() %>%
  add_candidates(tuned) %>%
  blend_predictions()

# However, fitting the models does not
fit <- blended %>%
  fit_members()
```

The above gets the error

``` Error in { : 
  task 1 failed - "`parameters` objects cannot be created from this type of object.
```

It works fine if I didn't include the `species = paste0(species, "-1")` step, and it breaks on every "wouldn't be a valid variable name" change I've made to the outcome.

### More detail

The traceback is:

```5.
stop(simpleError(msg, call = expr)) 
4.
e$fun(obj, substitute(ex), parent.frame(), e$data) 
3.
foreach::foreach(mem = member_names, .inorder = FALSE) %do_op% 
    {
        asNamespace("stacks")$fit_member(name = mem, wflows = model_stack[["model_defs"]], 
            members_map = members_map, train_dat = dat) ... at fit_members.R#118
2.
fit_members(.) 
1.
blended %>% fit_members() 
```

The foreach obscures the line where the error is happening, which is this step in `fit_member()`:

```
  member_params <- 
    wflows[[member_row$name.x[1]]] %>%
    dials::parameters() %>%
    dplyr::pull(id)
```

That happens because `member_row$name.x[1]` is NA, so `wflows[[member_row$name.x[1]]]` is NULL. With a little experimentation, I realized this happens because a join is failing whenever an outcome level isn't valid R syntax. (Something about sanitizing the class names doesn't seem to be working). That's basically where my understanding of the problem ends.

title: There are coefficients for models, but what about coefficients for variables/columns?
description:
In the documentation here https://stacks.tidymodels.org/reference/blend_predictions.html as well as documentation for `collect_parameters()` and `predict()`.
The first two discuss how the user can get the coefficients of the models. However, when sifting through the whole `stacks` documentation, I was unable to find how one can get coefficients for each of the variables/columns from the model stack with fitted resamples (using `fit_resamples`). I also tried looking through each of the model objects, but I was unable to find it (not the easiest thing to do to sift through various `stacks` objects).

So, is this even a possibility? How does `predict()` perform for a model stack (or 'a stacked ensemble model' object) without coefficients for each of the variables? Otherwise, I would like to request this feature.
(I asked on R Studio community a few times, but maybe it's because the package is rather new, not many people seem to be familiar, or the this feature is hard to catch)

``` r
#rm(list=ls())
library(tidyverse)
library(rsample)
library(lubridate)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'lubridate'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date, intersect, setdiff, union
library(tidymodels)
#> Registered S3 method overwritten by 'tune':
#>   method                   from   
#>   required_pkgs.model_spec parsnip
library(stacks)
library(baguette)
theme_set(theme_classic())

set.seed(123)

# Generate some data that increases over time
df <- data.frame(yearr = sample(2015:2021, 1000, replace = TRUE),
                 monthh = sample(1:12, 1000, replace = TRUE),
                 dayy = sample(1:29, 1000, replace = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(datee = ymd(paste(yearr, monthh, dayy)),
         weekk = week(datee),
         yy  = sample(10000:20000, 1000, replace = TRUE) + (yearr^2) + (2 * weekk)) |>
  filter(!is.na(datee)) |>
  arrange(-desc(datee))
#> Warning: 1 failed to parse.

folds = df |>
  sliding_period(lookback = Inf, # if Inf, then it's chain
                 period = 'week',
                 index = datee,
                 assess_stop = 1L, # include how many 'periods' in the future for training
                 every = 8L, # group how many 'periods' together
                 step = 2L, # how many 'periods' to move the window
                 skip = 8L) # skip how many first 'periods' for the model for assessment

###

rec_df = recipe(yy ~ ., data = df) 

rec_generic = rec_df |> # Recipe
  step_dummy(all_nominal()) |>
  step_zv(all_numeric(), all_outcomes()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric(), -all_outcomes()) |>
  update_role(datee, new_role = 'ID') |> # make dates not a predictor
  #step_rm(datee) |>
  step_zv(all_predictors())

metric = metric_set(rmse) # mae, or accuracy and roc_auc for classifications

grid_ctrl = control_stack_grid()
res_ctrl = control_stack_resamples()

### Elastic net
spec_enet = linear_reg(mode = 'regression', penalty = 0.1, mixture = 0.5) |> # penalty/mixture = varying() or tune()?
  set_engine('glmnet')

## add both to a workflow
wf_enet = workflow() |>
  add_model(spec_enet) |>
  add_recipe(rec_generic)

# fit to the folds
resample_enet = fit_resamples(wf_enet,
                              resamples = folds,
                              metrics = metric,
                              control = grid_ctrl)

###

### Bag Mars
spec_bag_mars = bag_mars() |>
  set_mode('regression') |>
  set_engine('earth')

wf_bag_mars = workflow() |>
  add_model(spec_bag_mars) |>
  add_recipe(rec_generic)

resample_bag_mars = fit_resamples(wf_bag_mars,
                                  resamples = folds,
                                  metrics = metric,
                                  control = res_ctrl)

### Put together the stacks
stack_candies = stacks() |>
  add_candidates(resample_enet) |>
  add_candidates(resample_bag_mars)

model_stack = stack_candies |>
  blend_predictions()

model_stack = model_stack |>
  fit_members()

# Weight of each model
rbind(
  model_stack |>
    collect_parameters('resample_bag_mars'),
  model_stack |>
    collect_parameters('resample_enet'))
#> # A tibble: 2 x 2
#>   member                 coef
#>   <chr>                 <dbl>
#> 1 resample_bag_mars_1_1 0    
#> 2 resample_enet_1_1     0.995

# Where are the coefficients for the covariates in model_stack?
df_pred = 
  df |>
  bind_cols(predict(model_stack, df)) |> # THIS PART HERE -- WHERE IS IT IN MODEL_STACK?
  rename(y_hat = .pred)
```

description:
Especially re: the # of dependency warnings since adding butcher methods, we should probably write out stringi. Uses of stringi in the package are usually

a. Relatively straightforward to replace with base R string functionality
b. Indicative of operations that could be carried out more robustly with dplyr 1.0.0

title: use previous resampling scheme
description:
Instead of use bootstrapping for the `glmnet` model, we should re-purpose the resampling scheme that the original models used. 

To do this, it might be enough to substitute the original `data` elements in the `splits` objects with the data stack tibble. The latter should have the same numebr of rows and we can ensure that the row order is the same.

title: make penalty an argument
description: Instead of use hardcoding a set of penalties, make it an argument and use the current values as the default.

title: resampling methods with multiple `id` columns
description:
Right now, it uses

```r
reconstruct_resamples(attr(data_stack, "splits"), dat)
```

You'll probably want to save the ID columns too since some resampling methods can have multiple id's. 

Also, `reconstruct_resamples()` doesn't set the `rsample` object's class correctly. Most of them have more specific classes than `rset` (such as "vfold_cv").

title: Integration with Modeltime
description:
Hey @simonpcouch & @topepo 

I'd like to open this issue to keep track of how I plan to use `stacks` within the `modeltime` forecasting framework. There shouldn't be anything additional required on your part to get the integration to happen. On my end, I'll just allow a `model_stack` that has been "fitted" (contains a "member_fits" list element) to be allowed in the `modeltime_table()`. 

Once `stacks` is released, just be aware that if you change the argument name or object class names, that it will break `modeltime` until I can catch up. 

---

## Plan 

The goal is to integrate `model_stack` objects into the `modeltime` forecasting workflow similar to how I integrate `workflow` objects. 

It's quite simple - add the fitted `model_stack` to a Modeltime Table just like you add a fitted `workflow`.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13734662/87168252-33ebce80-c29c-11ea-98bb-d9880a07769a.png)

Then the fitted model stack will follow the same forecasting workflow.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/13734662/87168505-993fbf80-c29c-11ea-9dec-d8b1e193c3d5.png)

To achieve this result, there are only a few requirements (things you need to be aware of that are intricacies of time series cross-validation and the `modeltime` forecasting workflow).

## Modeltime Forecasting Workflow Requirements:

- Objects must be "fitted" stacks, meaning you can call a `predict()` method and they work just like calling `predict(workflow, new_data)`. Therefore, there should be a way to easily determine if a stack has been fitted or not. __Only if a stack has been fitted, can it be added to a Modeltime Table.__ It looks like this can be detective if a model has a "member_fits" element.
- __Sequential models (e.g. ARIMA, Exponential Smoothing, RNN, LSTM) must be able to have stacks preserve the time-based sequence__. Note that this is only required for sequential models, and non-sequential models like Random Forest can use the normal cross-validation. This should be already taken care of with `rsample` and `timetk`. 
    - __Cross Validation:__ `rsample::rolling_origin()` or `timetk::time_series_cv()` as the grid tuning strategy
    - __Final Evaluation:__ `rsample::initial_time_split()` or `timetk::time_series_split()` as the final training and evaluation sets.

title: use of .config in stack_add
description:
A [post on stack overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/63202349/can-tidymodels-stacks-cover-models-with-differing-features-and-missing-values) yesterday points out a bug in `stack_add()`. 

``` r
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
#> ── Attaching packages ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────── tidymodels 0.1.1 ──
#> ✓ broom     0.7.0.9001     ✓ recipes   0.1.13    
#> ✓ dials     0.0.8          ✓ rsample   0.0.7     
#> ✓ infer     0.5.3.9000     ✓ tune      0.1.1.9000
#> ✓ modeldata 0.0.2          ✓ workflows 0.1.2     
#> ✓ parsnip   0.1.2          ✓ yardstick 0.0.7
#> ── Conflicts ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── tidymodels_conflicts() ──
#> x scales::discard() masks purrr::discard()
#> x dplyr::filter()   masks stats::filter()
#> x recipes::fixed()  masks stringr::fixed()
#> x dplyr::lag()      masks stats::lag()
#> x yardstick::spec() masks readr::spec()
#> x recipes::step()   masks stats::step()
library(workflows)
library(probably)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'probably'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     as.factor, as.ordered
library(tune)
library(stacks)

set.seed(1234)

mtcars_tb <- mtcars %>% 
  as_tibble() %>% 
  mutate(vs = c(sample(vs, 0), rep(NA_integer_, 10), sample(vs, 22)),
         disp = c(sample(disp, 22), rep(NA_integer_, 10)))

train_test_split <- initial_split(mtcars_tb)
train <- training(train_test_split)
test <- testing(train_test_split)

cv_fold_mtc <- vfold_cv(mtcars_tb)

recipe_naomit <- recipe(mpg ~ disp + vs, data = train) %>% 
  step_naomit(all_predictors(), skip = TRUE) %>%
  step_normalize(all_numeric()) 

ctrl_grid <- control_stack_grid()
ctrl_res <- control_stack_resamples()

lasso_mod <- 
  linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("glmnet") %>% 
  set_args(penalty = tune(),
           mixture = 1)

wflow <-
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(recipe_naomit) %>%
  add_model(lasso_mod)

lasso_tune <- 
  tune_grid(
    object = wflow, 
    resamples = cv_fold_mtc, 
    grid = 10,
    control = ctrl_grid
  )
#> The workflow being saved contains a recipe, which is 0.01 Mb in memory. If this was not intentional, please set the control setting `save_workflow = FALSE`.

model_st <- stacks() %>%
  stack_add(lasso_tune)
#> Warning: Values are not uniquely identified; output will contain list-cols.
#> * Use `values_fn = list` to suppress this warning.
#> * Use `values_fn = length` to identify where the duplicates arise
#> * Use `values_fn = {summary_fun}` to summarise duplicates
```

This traces back to the use of the `.config` column in the `collect_predictions()` call from [`.set_data_candidates()`](https://github.com/tidymodels/stacks/blob/8a4d134783cf548866c6083c07bbc115f56af59d/R/stack_add.R#L196-L221). The code currently assumes that the `.config` and `.row` columns in the output of `collect_predictions` with `summarize = TRUE` should uniquely identify a row. This is not the case, though:

``` r
collect_predictions(lasso_tune, summarize = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 320 x 5
#>     .row  penalty   mpg .config .pred
#>    <int>    <dbl> <dbl> <fct>   <dbl>
#>  1     1 1.39e-10 0.111 Model01   NaN
#>  2     1 1.21e- 9 0.111 Model02   NaN
#>  3     1 5.95e- 8 0.111 Model03   NaN
#>  4     1 4.81e- 7 0.111 Model04   NaN
#>  5     1 1.08e- 6 0.111 Model05   NaN
#>  6     1 3.43e- 5 0.111 Model06   NaN
#>  7     1 7.28e- 4 0.111 Model07   NaN
#>  8     1 7.05e- 3 0.111 Model08   NaN
#>  9     1 5.62e- 2 0.111 Model09   NaN
#> 10     1 3.46e- 1 0.111 Model08   NaN
#> # … with 310 more rows
```

<sup>Created on 2020-08-02 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0.9001)</sup>

I'm not sure this is a fair assumption to make—@juliasilge, is the `.config` column here functioning as expected? I'm surprised to see two entries for `Model08`, `.row` 1 (rows 8 10 in the reprex above). Will adjust the assumptions `stack_add()` makes if so! :-)

title: control stack grid error - save prediction and workflow
description:
Trying to run a basic example of stacks that is  highly similar to the vignettes. I receive this error on `control_stack_grid` 
```r
ctrl_grid<- control_stack_grid()
```

**Error in tune::control_grid(save_pred = TRUE, save_workflow = TRUE) : 
  unused argument (save_workflow = TRUE)**

It seems like we must tune using `control_stack_*()` to add candidates to the stack down the line, so this impedes adding candidates.

title: add a specific check to see if the workflow (and predictions) were saved
description: I forgot to tune with `save_workflow` and got a complex error message. We should recommend using the specific options that they need.

title: remove candidates with identical predictions
description:
Probably at the `.set_data_candidates` stage, but possibly later, make sure to check that there are no two models whose predictions are identical. A computationally reasonable way to do this a la `finetune`:
  
```

    tmp <- x[, !(names(x) %in% ids)]
    exclude <- c(exclude, names(tmp[duplicated(lapply(tmp, c))]))
    x <- x[, !(names(x) %in% exclude)]

```

My leaning here is to just drop that candidate and warn the user, but I could see the argument for erroring out.

title: Update example objects
description:
After having these around for a couple weeks, a few thoughts on how the example model objects exported with the package can be most helpful:

* The objects should be able to be regenerated relatively quickly (and be saved as `.Rda` + loaded during testing as they are now, rather than regenerated in testing)
* The grids that models are tuned on should be as thin as possible while still introducing diversity into the ensemble
* Use engines and model types that won't cause dependency / GHA install headaches

As for the dataset underlying them:

* 1 factor variable with 3 classes, relatively balanced
* 1 factor variable with 2 classes, relatively balanced
* A few numeric variables
* Both of the factors should be somewhat difficult to predict—ROCs in the 80s or so with simple models
* 200 - 500 rows
* No missing values

Will get back to this once thesis meetings start up!

title: save some metrics for the glmnet model
description: We should have an a tibble with the results of `collect_metrics()` that the user can look at to assess performance and choice of `penalty`.

title: warn rather than error on identical predictions
description:
Related to #23.

Will require some checks further upstream in the `add_candidates()` `.set` pipeline than is currently the case.

title: function to match id with hyperparameters
description:
There should be some way to match up the `.config` for a member with its hyperparameters, metrics, and stacking coefficients.

Possibly something along the lines up `collect_parameters`?

title: add butcher methods
description: To trim out extra stuff that is not needed to make predictions.

title: document how to update example objects
description: Possibly a vignette along the lines of "how to contribute to stacks"... some sort of resource noting the `man-roxygen` procedure + testing strategy.

title: edit docs organization in pkgdown yaml
description:
The "main verbs" should be at the forefront, and then helpers + methods for the fitted object.

Related to #31.

title: validation sets
description:
With `rsample`, validation sets are structured a little bit differently. You never get hold-out predictions on the entire training set, just the assessment set. When we assemble the data stack, we can't just substitute that data into the previous resampling strategy since we only have assessment set predictions (and that isn't helpful for tuning the `glmnet` model). 

I suggest creating a brand new bootstrap object for the data when, originally, a validation set was used (like you originally had).

title: General thoughts and suggestions on stacks
description:
Hi @simonpcouch,

Cool new package! I've been playing around with it for a little and I like the API a lot and I have a few suggestions/comments:

- I think the documentation for `blend_predictions()` can be improved by spending a few sentences explaining a little more about what happens under-the-hood (i.e. a LASSO is fit to 25 bootstrap resamples of the `as_tibble(data_stack)` object passed to `blend_predictions()`). I figured things out by looking into the source code, but without doing that it was a little opaque about what exactly was going on to get the stacking weights.

- Also I'm wondering if it might be worth specifically noting in the documentation that the `weights` are betas/coefficients from the LASSO. 

- Semantics: `Out of 15 possible blending coefficients, the ensemble used 5.` I wonder if its clearer to use retained/identified/selected instead of _used_ in this context? Or maybe even `Out of 15 possible sub-models, the ensemble includes 5.`. I'm just thinking out loud.

- Even after playing around with the functions I'm still not crystal clear on `fit_members()` purpose. The documentation does little to resolve my confusion. I think this function specifically could use some documentation improvements.

- The `Example Data` section is very informative, but it appears in so many of the help docs for various functions that it sorta obfuscates the documentation relevant specifically to that function. Just an observation.

title: Parallel Processing Considerations - Blend Predictions, Tune Grid Control
description:
Just adding a note here to consider parallel processing when using [`tune_grid`](https://github.com/tidymodels/stacks/blob/41300420415556553a9078c7d281b8800f720fe8/R/blend_predictions.R#L135). 

A possible way to handle is to elevate / create an extension of the `tune::control_grid()` to the function that allows access to the `allow_par` argument:

```
blend_predictions <- function(data_stack, penalty = 10 ^ (-6:-1), verbose = FALSE, ..., control = control_blend(allow_par = TRUE)) {...}
```

Where `control_blend` is:

```
#' @export 
control_blend <- function(verbose = FALSE, allow_par = TRUE, pkgs = NULL) {
   get_models <- function(x) {
      x %>% 
          workflows::pull_workflow_fit() %>% 
          purrr::pluck("fit")
    }

    tune::control_grid(save_pred = TRUE, extract = get_models, verbose = verbose, allow_par = allow_par, pkgs = pkgs)
}
```

title: Error when adding candidates to stacks: stacks expected a tibble but got a data frame
description:
## The problem

I'm getting an error when trying to add a candidate to stacks(). The error has to do with an element of the tune object being a data frame when stacks was expecting it to be a tibble. Manually converting that object to a tibble fixes the problem. I am using the latest development version of the tune package.

## Highlight

```r
# Throws an error
attrition_stack <- stacks() %>%
  add_candidates(rf_tune)
#> Error: Element `attr(data_stack, "train")` needs to inherit from `tbl_df`, but its class is `data.frame`.

# Can be fixed with:
rf_tune$splits[[1]][[1]] <- as_tibble(rf_tune$splits[[1]][[1]])

attrition_stack <- stacks() %>%
  add_candidates(rf_tune)
```

## Full Reproducible example

```r
library(tidyverse)
suppressMessages(library(tidymodels))
library(modeldata)
suppressMessages(library(themis))
library(embed)
library(stacks)

data(attrition)

attrition <- janitor::clean_names(attrition)

attrition <- attrition %>% 
  mutate(attrition_class = fct_rev(attrition)) %>% 
  select(-attrition)

levels(attrition$attrition_class)
#> [1] "Yes" "No"

set.seed(2020)
attrition_split <- initial_split(attrition, strata = "attrition_class")
attrition_train <- training(attrition_split)
attrition_test <- testing(attrition_split)
attrition_folds <- vfold_cv(attrition_train, v = 5, strata = "attrition_class")

rf_recipe <- 
  recipe(formula = attrition_class ~ ., data = attrition_train)

rf_spec <- 
  rand_forest(mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), trees = 500) %>% 
  set_mode("classification") %>% 
  set_engine("ranger") 

rf_workflow <- 
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(rf_recipe) %>% 
  add_model(rf_spec) 

rf_grid <- grid_latin_hypercube(
  finalize(mtry(), select(attrition_train, -attrition_class)),
  min_n(),
  size = 10
)

set.seed(1551)
rf_tune <-
  tune_grid(rf_workflow,
            resamples = attrition_folds,
            grid = rf_grid,
            control = control_stack_grid(),
            metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, pr_auc, f_meas, sens, spec, j_index, mcc, accuracy))
```

title: Sub-models terminology change suggestion
description:
Hi there!  Very cool to see stacking in Tidymodels!  

I will take a deeper look at the package soon, but I wanted to share my thoughts about the terminology used -- specifically around the term _sub-models_.  Traditionally, in the stacking literature and community, those models are referred to as _base models_.  The term _sub-models_  has been used more specifically in the "Divide and Recombine" sense, namely, when you train models on a subsets/partitions of the original training set and then ensemble them together.  

I can provide more context or sources if you need it.

title: Stacks can´t add_candidates
description:
## The problem

I'm having trouble with stacks in add candidates. I had the error message:
Erro: Element `attr(data_stack, "train")` needs to inherit from `tbl_df`, but its class is `data.frame`.
Run `rlang::last_error()` to see where the error occurred.

## Reproducible example

```r
library(tidyverse)
library(arsenal)
library(lubridate)
library(tidymodels)
library(vip)
library(stacks)

durval <- read.csv('durval_final.csv', stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
                   sep = ';', dec = ',')

durval_anal <- durval %>% 
  select(idade, sc_receptor, cor, sexo, tipo_dialise, d_base, diabetes,
         PRA_I, re_tx, mismatchs, idade_doador, sexo_doador,
         cor_doador, imc_doador, causa_morte, has_doador, dm_doador,
         Na_doador, cpk_doador, creat_doador_final, DVA, TIF,
         tempo_anastomose, inducao, DGF)


## Split Data -----------------------------------------------------

set.seed(123)
split <- initial_split(durval_anal, prop = 0.75)
durval_train <- training(split)
durval_test <- testing(split)

## -- Analise Recipe ---------------------------------------------

rec_lasso <- recipe(DGF ~ . , data = durval_train) %>% 
  step_rm(sexo, sexo_doador, cor, cor_doador, re_tx, mismatchs, d_base, tipo_dialise, inducao) %>% 
  step_BoxCox(all_numeric()) %>% 
  step_medianimpute(all_numeric()) %>% 
  step_center(all_numeric()) %>% 
  step_scale(all_numeric()) %>% 
  step_corr(all_numeric(), threshold = 0.9) %>% 
  step_ns(TIF, creat_doador_final, deg_free = 4) %>% 
  step_dummy(all_nominal(), -all_outcomes()) %>% 
  step_nzv(all_predictors())

rec_tree <- recipe(DGF ~ . , data = durval_train) %>% 
  step_rm(sexo, sexo_doador, cor, cor_doador, re_tx, mismatchs, d_base, tipo_dialise, inducao) %>% 
  step_medianimpute(all_numeric()) %>% 
  step_dummy(all_nominal(), -all_outcomes(), one_hot = TRUE) %>% 
  step_nzv(all_predictors())


## --- Model -----------------------------------------------------

model_lasso <- logistic_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = tune()) %>% 
  set_engine('glmnet')

model_xgb <- boost_tree(mode = 'classification', mtry = tune(), min_n = tune(), tree_depth = tune(), loss_reduction = tune()) %>% 
  set_engine('xgboost')


## --- workflow ---------------------------------------------------

work_lasso <- workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(rec_lasso) %>% 
  add_model(model_lasso)

work_xgb <- workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(rec_tree) %>% 
  add_model(model_xgb)

## --- folds -----------------------------------------------------

set.seed(123)
folds <- bootstraps(durval_train, times = 10)

## --- tunes ---------------------------------------------------

doParallel::registerDoParallel()

set.seed(123)
tune_lasso <- tune_grid(
  work_lasso,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = 15,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy),
  control = control_stack_grid()
)

set.seed(123)
tune_xgb <- tune_grid(
  work_xgb,
  resamples = folds,
  grid = 10,
  metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, accuracy),
  control = control_stack_grid()
)


stack01 <- stacks() %>% 
  add_candidates(tune_lasso) %>% 
  add_candidates(tune_xgb)
```

title: Error: `in_id` must be a positive integer vector
description:
I'm not sure if this is a feature request or a request for help, but I'm getting an error with `blend_predictions()`, and I wonder if it is possible to make this message more informative. Maybe it's plenty informative but I don't have a good grasp of stacks. 

(I posted a [separate stacks issue to RStudio Community](https://community.rstudio.com/t/stacks-model-doesnt-make-use-of-the-same-resampling-object-as-the-existing-candidates/86264?u=ericpgreen) with reprex that is more squarely in the "help please" camp)

> Error: `in_id` must be a positive integer vector.

My data stack tibble has the following:

```
# A data stack with 8 model definitions and 646 candidate members:
#   fpv_res_multinom_glmnet: 55 sub-models
#   fpv_res_rf: 125 sub-models
#   fpv_res_knn: 25 sub-models
#   fpv_res_bt: 125 sub-models
#   fpv_res_klr: 25 sub-models
#   fpv_res_mars: 152 sub-models
#   fpv_res_nb: 25 sub-models
```

What is `in_id`, and what are some reasons why it would not be a positive integer vector? I can see it in the output of `str(myStack)`, but I'm not sure what to make of it.

title: Error in classification stack when outcome variable contains white space
description:
## The problem

I ran into a small issue when trying a classification stack with an outcome variable that included a space in the factor label. Specifically, I was using the stackoverflow data from `modeldata` that has a binary outcome variable with levels "Remote" and "Not Remote". The latter seems to cause the `blend_predictions` step to not be able to identify the model type, which consequently causes `fit_members` to fail with the error:

> Error in {: task 1 failed - "`parameters` objects cannot be created from this type of object."

Maybe `blend_predictions` could throw a warning about the white space, or replace white space with an underscore to avoid the error? 

Thanks for the great package by the way!

## Reproducible example

``` r
library(modeldata)
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(stacks)  

set.seed(12)
data("stackoverflow")

# initial split
split <- initial_split(stackoverflow, prop = 0.75, strata = "Remote")
train <- training(split)
test <- testing(split)

folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(train, v = 5) 

rec <- recipe(Remote ~ ., data = train) %>%
  step_dummy(Country, one_hot = TRUE) 

stackof_wf <- 
  workflow() %>% 
  add_recipe(rec)

ctrl_res <- control_stack_resamples()

rand_forest_spec <- 
  rand_forest(
    trees = 500
  ) %>%
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("ranger")

rand_forest_wflow <-
  stackof_wf %>%
  add_model(rand_forest_spec)

rand_forest_res <- 
  fit_resamples(
    object = rand_forest_wflow, 
    resamples = folds, 
    control = ctrl_res
  )

nnet_spec <-
  mlp() %>%
  set_mode("classification") %>%
  set_engine("nnet")

nnet_rec <- 
  rec %>% 
  step_normalize(all_predictors())

nnet_wflow <- 
  stackof_wf %>%
  add_model(nnet_spec) %>% 
  update_recipe(nnet_rec)

nnet_res <-
  fit_resamples(
    object = nnet_wflow, 
    resamples = folds, 
    control = ctrl_res
  )

stackof_st <- 
  # initialize the stack
  stacks() %>%
  # add candidate members
  add_candidates(rand_forest_res) %>%
  add_candidates(nnet_res)  %>% 
  blend_predictions()
```

title: Non-linear metalearning algorithms
description:
## Non-linear metalearning algorithms

_Hey, sorry I meant to post this about a month ago when I was first exploring the package, and then I got lost in the election drama and forgot to follow up. :-/  I saw that stacks just made it to CRAN (congrats!) so it reminded me to write it up and post here (I had hoped to provide this feedback before it went to CRAN)._

The structure of the output objects (as well as the language used in the docs) presumes that a linear model will be used for the metalearning algorithm (there's a focus & dependency on there being coefficients/weights for the base learners).  In the [`blend_predictions()`](https://stacks.tidymodels.org/reference/blend_predictions.html) function, the metalearner algorithm is pre-specified as a Lasso GLM (not configurable to the user).  In general, stacking can use any type of supervised algorithm as the metalearner (blending algorithm), so even if you choose to hard-code the algo to using a Lasso GLM for a metalearning algorithm, it might be worth considering (maybe you have already?) whether you want to add some abstraction layer so that the structure of the output does not depend on the ensemble being a linear/weighted stack of the base models (in case you want to extend the functionality later).  Do you have plans to extend this to any type of algorithm for a metalearner, or do you see this being a fixed component of the stacking implementation in **stacks**?

While a GLM with some regularization is my go-to metalearner as well (and the default in H2O's Stacked Ensemble algo), there are a lot of cases where other algorithms will produce a better stacked ensemble (see Kaggle for examples).  In [`h2o::h2o.stackedEnsemble()`](http://docs.h2o.ai/h2o/latest-stable/h2o-r/docs/reference/h2o.stackedEnsemble.html), we allow the user to customize the metalearning algorithm, and we use an Elastic-Net GLM as the default.  Metalearner flexibility is also offered in the original stacking R package, [SuperLearner](https://github.com/ecpolley/SuperLearner), via the `method` argument (defaults to linear model fit via non-negative least squares).  I think there's a lot of utility in allowing people to customize their metalearning method (and removing the dependency on linear models).

**Summary:** If you had planned to allow the user to specify their own metalearner at some point in the future (or want to keep the option open), it might be worth re-structuring the output to remove the dependency on having a linear model for metalearning.   

**Recommendation for docs:** Right now it reads as if GLM as the metalearner is an unchangeable or native aspect of the the stacked ensemble algorithm, so it might be good to add some extra context for the reader who is new to stacking to clarify that this is just one algo that can be used for metalearning.
